title: Suffixes and parts of speech
blurb: Use a word's ending to tell its part of speech and its category, and choose the right form of a word for a sentence.
question: A TEAS item asks which word correctly completes the sentence "Before the procedure, the technician must ___ the instruments," offering sterility, sterile, sterilely and sterilize. How does the suffix tell you which form fits?

teach.h: The ending tells you the job
teach.body: Formally, a suffix is a word part attached to the end of a root or base word that often shows the word's part of speech or category: a noun, a person, an adjective, a verb, an adverb, a condition or a procedure. In plain English: the root says what the word is about, and the suffix says what job the word does in a sentence. Change the suffix and the same idea becomes a thing, a quality or an action.

teach.caption: The core idea stays the same; only the job in the sentence changes.
-ful and -less are opposites. An assistant is a person; assistance is the help given.

teach.h: Choosing the right form for a blank
items: Look at the slot: after 'a,' 'an' or 'the' you usually need a noun.
After 'to' or a helping verb such as 'must' or 'can,' you need a verb (-ize, -ify, -ate, -en).
Describing a noun, or after 'is' or 'seems,' you need an adjective (-able, -al, -ous, -ful).
Describing how an action is done, you usually need an adverb (-ly).

teach.body: Kevin Nguyen, applying to a surgical technology program, sees: 'After the flood, the town had to ___ its water supply.' Options: purity, pure, purely, purify. The blank follows 'had to,' so it needs a verb. Purity ends in -ity (noun), pure is an adjective, purely ends in -ly (adverb). Purify ends in -ify, a verb suffix meaning 'to make': to make pure. Kevin picks purify.

teach.text: The TEAS often offers the right root with the wrong suffix, so every option 'means' the same thing but only one does the right job. Also watch -er: it can name a person (donor, worker) or compare (faster). And -ly is usually, not always, an adverb.

items: Match the suffix to the slot in the sentence.

summary: You can now read a suffix to tell whether a word is a noun, a person, an adjective, a verb or an adverb. You can also pick the form of a word that fits a sentence and avoid look-alike endings such as -ful/-less and -ant/-ance.

A.q: Which suffix turns the verb "treat" into a noun?
A.why: -ment forms nouns of act or result: treatment.

whyNot.2: -ly forms an adverb, not a noun.
whyNot.3: -ize forms verbs, and treat is already a verb.

A.q: In which word does the suffix mean "without"?
A.why: -less means without: painless means without pain.

whyNot.0: -ful means full of, the opposite of -less.

A.q: Based on its suffix, which word is an adjective?
A.why: -ary is an adjective suffix meaning relating to: sanitary describes something.

whyNot.0: -ity forms a noun of state or quality.
whyNot.3: -ist forms a noun naming a person.

B.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? "Before the procedure, the technician must ___ the instruments."
B.why: After the helping verb 'must,' the sentence needs a verb. -ize is a verb suffix meaning to make: sterilize means to make sterile.

whyNot.0: -ity makes a noun (the state of being sterile), which cannot follow 'must.'
whyNot.1: Sterile is an adjective; it describes but cannot act as the verb.
whyNot.2: -ly makes an adverb, which describes how an action is done.

B.q: In "cardiologist," the suffix -logist tells you that the word names
B.why: -logist means a specialist, a person who studies or practices in a field: a cardiologist specializes in the heart.

whyNot.0: A disease would use a suffix such as -pathy or -itis.
whyNot.1: A procedure would use a suffix such as -ectomy or -scopy.
whyNot.3: The study area is -logy (cardiology); -logist is the person.

B.q: Which word in this sentence is an adverb? "The careful nurse quickly checked the sterile dressing."
B.why: -ly usually marks an adverb, and quickly describes how the nurse checked.

whyNot.0: -ful forms an adjective: careful describes the nurse.
whyNot.2: Sterile is an adjective describing the dressing.
whyNot.3: Dressing is a noun, the object being checked.

C.q: Based on its suffix, which word names a PERSON?
C.why: -ant can mean a person who: an assistant is a person who assists.

whyNot.1: -ance forms a noun of state or act: assistance is the help, not the helper.

C.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? "Lack of sleep can ___ the body's defenses against infection."
C.why: After the helping verb 'can,' a verb is needed. -en is a verb suffix meaning to make or become: weaken.

whyNot.0: -ness forms a noun, which cannot follow 'can' as the action.

C.q: In which pair do the suffixes create OPPOSITE meanings?
C.why: -ful means full of and -less means without, so painful and painless are opposites.

whyNot.0: -ment (noun) and -able (adjective) change the part of speech, not the direction of meaning.
whyNot.1: -er (comparative) and -est (superlative) are degrees of the same quality.
whyNot.2: -ify and -ize are both verb suffixes meaning to make.

reteach.title: Same actor, different roles
reteach.question: Picture an actor who plays a different role in every film. How is a suffix like the costume that tells you the role?

blocks.body: The root is the actor: 'pain' is always about pain. The suffix is the costume. Dressed as -ful, pain becomes a describing word (painful). Dressed as -less, it describes the opposite (painless). Add -ly and it describes how something is done (painlessly). You recognize the role from the costume, even before you know the plot.

blocks.text: Some costumes look alike: an assistant (-ant) is a person, but assistance (-ance) is the help itself.

explain.body: -tion, -sion, -ment, -ness, -ity, -ance, -ence, -ism, -ship, -hood and -dom name a state, act or quality. -er, -or, -ist, -ian, -ant and -ent name a person who does something.

test.q: Based on its suffix, which word is a noun?
test.why: -ness forms a noun naming a state: illness.

whyNot.2: -ful forms an adjective meaning full of.
whyNot.3: -en forms a verb meaning to make or become.

test.q: Based on its suffix, a "treatable" condition is one that
test.why: -able means able to be, so treatable means able to be treated.

whyNot.0: -able describes what is possible, not something already done.
whyNot.1: Without treatment would need a suffix such as -less.
whyNot.3: -able means able to be, the opposite of resisting.

explain.body: -ize, -ify, -ate and -en form verbs meaning to make or become (sterilize, purify, hydrate, weaken). -ly usually forms an adverb (rapidly).

test.q: Which suffix turns the adjective "sterile" into a verb?
test.why: -ize is a verb suffix meaning to make: sterilize means to make sterile.

explain.body: -er can name a person who does something (worker, teacher) or form a comparative meaning 'more' (faster). -est forms the superlative meaning 'most' (fastest).

test.q: In which sentence does a word end in -er as a comparative, meaning "more"?
test.why: Faster means more fast: here -er is the comparative ending.

whyNot.0: Teacher uses -er to name a person who teaches.
whyNot.1: Worker uses -er to name a person who works.
whyNot.3: Runner uses -er to name a person who runs.
